en: Nuri is a space rocket that Korea made by itself. A launch vehicle is a rocket that carries satellites into space. The name Nuri was chosen by the people of Korea. Researchers at Korea's space center studied it for more than ten years. Korean technology did it all, from design to building.

In June 2022, the second Nuri launch was a success. It put a test satellite into orbit around Earth. In May 2023, the third launch also worked well. This time it carried several real working satellites. The satellites reached orbit and began their jobs.

The success of Nuri means a lot to Korea. Only a few countries can launch heavy satellites by themselves. In 2024, Korea opened a new space agency. Now the country has an office to lead its space work. The agency is in Sacheon, a city in the south.

Space work needs the effort of many people. Engineers design the rocket and scientists study the satellites. Experts who study data on computers help too. Nuri is the fruit of their hard work. The challenge to reach space still goes on today.

en: Every living thing has genes inside its body. Genes are a plan that decides how a living thing looks. If the plan changes, the living thing changes too. CRISPR is a tool that cuts one chosen part of the plan. It cuts like scissors, so people call it gene scissors.

CRISPR was found while scientists studied bacteria. Bacteria can fight viruses that attack them. They remember a piece of the virus they fought before. If the same virus comes again, they cut that piece. Scientists turned this idea into a tool for fixing genes.

Two scientists won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Today this tool is used in many places. Doctors study ways to treat diseases caused by genes. Farmers also use it to grow crops that fight disease. A new road to help sick people is open.

But we must also be careful. A wrong change in a gene can bring surprise problems. So scientists make rules and work slowly and carefully. A new tool needs wise hands. How we use CRISPR is a question for everyone.

en: Today AI can answer questions and even write. It can also make song words and stories. We call this kind of AI generative AI. It makes new things like writing and pictures. So how does a computer write like this?

Generative AI learns by reading a huge amount of writing. It studies how words follow words in books and news. Then it guesses which word comes next. For example, after the word clear, the word sky is likely. It keeps guessing this way until a long text is done.

But AI does not really understand meaning like people do. So it sometimes says wrong things in a smart way. It may even make up a book that does not exist. An AI answer is not always the right answer.

Generative AI is a good tool for study and life. It helps with writing practice and finding answers. But you must check important facts again. It is good to compare them with books you can trust. The power to use tools wisely is more and more important.

challenge.q: 글쓴이가 '미리 준비하는 일이 더욱 중요하다'라고 말한 까닭으로 가장 알맞은 것은?
choices: 노인의 수가 갑자기 줄어들 수 있기 때문에
실버산업이 새로운 일자리를 많이 만들기 때문에
학교가 한번 문을 닫으면 다시 열 수 없기 때문에
인구의 변화는 천천히 일어나서 짧은 시간에 바꾸기 어렵기 때문에
challenge.explain: 글의 마지막 문단은 인구의 변화가 아주 천천히 일어난다고 말한 뒤 미리 준비해야 한다고 했다. 천천히 일어나는 변화는 문제를 알아차린 뒤에 짧은 시간에 바꾸기 어렵기 때문이다. ②는 본문에 나오는 내용이지만, 미리 준비해야 하는 까닭과는 관계가 없다.

en: In Korea, fewer babies are born each year. At the same time, the number of old people grows fast. Better medicine helps people live much longer. When the share of old people grows, we call it aging. Korea is one of the fastest aging countries in the world.

Aging changes a country in big ways. Some schools close because there are fewer students. The number of young workers goes down too. But the work of caring for old people grows. So a country spends its money in new ways.

These changes are not only hard. More hospitals and care homes for old people open. Companies make things that are easy for old people to use. This business of goods and care for old people is called the silver industry. New jobs are born from this change.

The government is getting ready for this change. It makes plans to help families with young children. It also supports jobs and health for old people. A change in population happens very slowly. So getting ready early is even more important.

Korea is one of the fastest
So a country spends its money
This business of goods and care

questions.q: 이 글의 중심 내용으로 가장 알맞은 것은?

questions.q: 이 글을 읽고 짐작할 수 있는 것은?

challenge.q: 이 글의 원리에 따를 때, 아이스크림 값이 내려갈 상황으로 가장 알맞은 것은?
choices: 무더위가 와서 아이스크림을 사려는 사람이 갑자기 많아졌다.
공장이 늘어 아이스크림은 많아졌는데 사려는 사람은 줄었다.
아이스크림을 만드는 재료의 값이 올라 만들기가 어려워졌다.
한국은행이 금리를 내려 시중에 돈이 더 많이 돌게 되었다.
challenge.explain: 글에서 물건이 많은데 사려는 사람이 적으면 값이 내린다고 했으므로, 아이스크림은 많아지고 사려는 사람은 준 상황이 답이다. 사려는 사람이 갑자기 많아진 상황은 오히려 값이 오르는 경우라서 헷갈리기 쉽지만 반대의 결과가 나온다. 재료 값이 올라 만들기 어려워지면 물건이 줄어드는 쪽이므로 값이 내려갈 상황이 아니다.

같은 돈으로 살 수 있는 물건의 수가 전보다 늘어날 것이다.
한국은행은 시중에 돈이 더 많이 돌게 하여 물가를 관리할 것이다.
최저임금위원회는 임금을 정할 때 오른 물가를 살펴볼 것이다.
challenge.explain: 글에서 최저임금은 물가와 생활비 등을 두루 살펴서 정한다고 했으므로, 물가가 크게 오르면 위원회가 이를 살펴볼 것이라고 짐작할 수 있다. 한국은행이 나온다는 점에서 세 번째 선지가 헷갈리지만, 한국은행은 물가가 안정되도록 관리한다고 했을 뿐 돈을 더 많이 돌게 한다는 내용은 글에 없다. 또 물가가 오르면 같은 돈으로 살 수 있는 물건은 오히려 줄어든다.

en: Everything we buy has a price. When we put many prices together, we call it the price level. When the price level rises, the same money buys less. If snacks cost more, you can buy fewer snacks. Prices that keep going up are called inflation.

A price changes with buyers and sellers. If buyers are many and goods are few, the price goes up. If goods are many and buyers are few, the price goes down. We call this the rule of demand and supply.

Life gets hard when prices rise too fast. So the Bank of Korea works to keep prices steady. It watches how much money moves around the country. It also moves the interest rate up or down. Interest is the price you pay to borrow money.

The money you earn from work is called a wage. The lowest wage set by law is the minimum wage. A special committee sets the minimum wage every year. Workers, companies, and public members meet and talk about it. They look at prices and living costs before they decide.

we call it the price level.
the rule of demand and supply.
So the Bank of Korea works

challenge.explain: 바다 쓰레기의 많은 부분은 땅에서 시작되어 강을 타고 바다로 간다고 했으므로, 땅에서 쓰레기를 덜 만들면 바다로 가는 쓰레기도 줄어든다. 플라스틱은 잘 썩지 않는 재료라고 했으므로 '빨리 썩게 한다'는 틀렸고, 일회용품을 줄이더라도 이미 버려진 쓰레기를 줍는 정화 활동은 여전히 필요하므로 그 선지도 알맞지 않다.

en: Plastic trash on the street washes into rivers with rain and wind. Rivers carry the trash all the way to the sea. So much of the sea trash starts on land. Some trash is also thrown away at the beach. Fishing tools and boat trash can stay in the sea.
Plastic does not rot easily. Plastic in the sea stays there for many, many years. Waves and sunlight only break it into smaller pieces. Pieces smaller than five millimeters are called microplastic.

Sea animals have a hard time because of plastic. A sea turtle may eat a bag, thinking it is a jellyfish. Birds eat small bits of plastic as if it were food. Microplastic is found inside fish and shellfish too. Some animals get caught in nets and get hurt.

Many people are working to solve this problem. People clean up trash together on beaches. The country also collects trash from the sea. Using fewer one-time things and sorting trash well helps a lot. Saving the sea starts with small actions.

온실가스는 지구의 온도를 알맞게 지켜 주는 일도 하기 때문이다.

challenge.explain: 4문단에서 흐린 날에는 태양광 발전이 어렵기 때문에 전기를 모아 두는 저장 기술이 함께 연구되고 있다고 했다. 이 마을은 낮에 만든 전기를 모아 두었다가 흐린 날에 썼으므로 저장 기술을 활용한 것이다. 전기를 덜 쓴 것이 아니라 모아 두었다가 쓴 것이므로 '아껴 쓰는 작은 습관'은 답이 될 수 없다.

en: The Earth is wrapped in air, like a blanket. Gases in the air, like carbon dioxide, hold the Earth's heat. We call these gases greenhouse gases. Thanks to them, the Earth stays warm enough. But too much gas makes the Earth hotter and hotter.

We burn fuels like coal and oil. This makes a lot of greenhouse gas. Power plants and cars make it too. A hotter Earth changes the weather and melts glaciers. So many countries promised to cut these gases. Carbon neutral means the gas we send out equals the gas we take in.

For carbon neutral, people look to renewable energy. Renewable energy comes from nature and can be used again. Solar power makes electricity from sunlight. Wind power turns big blades to make electricity. Water power uses running water to make electricity too.

But there are problems too. Solar power is hard on cloudy days. Wind power stops when the wind does not blow. So people also study ways to store electricity. Small habits, like saving electricity, help protect the Earth.
enseg: equals the gas we take in.
when the wind does not blow.

questions.explain: 첫째 문단에서 왕도 기록을 볼 수 없었기에 사관이 사실을 있는 그대로 남길 수 있었다고 하였다.

challenge.q: 이 글에서 조선이 실록을 지킨 방법과 가장 비슷한 것은?
choices: 소중한 사진을 튼튼한 금고 한 곳에 넣고 자물쇠를 채운다.
소중한 사진을 컴퓨터, USB, 인터넷에 각각 저장해 둔다.
소중한 사진을 매일 꺼내 보며 깨끗하게 닦아 둔다.
소중한 사진을 잃어버리지 않게 늘 몸에 지니고 다닌다.
challenge.explain: 조선은 같은 실록을 여러 벌 만들어 멀리 떨어진 사고에 나누어 두었다. 한 곳이 불타도 다른 곳의 책이 남기 때문이다. 튼튼한 금고에 넣는 것은 안전해 보이지만 한 곳에만 두는 것이라, 그곳에 불이 나면 전부 잃게 되므로 이 글의 방법과 다르다.

challenge.q: 만약 왕이 사관의 기록을 마음대로 볼 수 있었다면 어떤 일이 생겼을까?
choices: 사관이 왕의 눈치를 보느라 사실을 그대로 적기 어려웠을 것이다.
실록이 지금보다 훨씬 빨리 완성되었을 것이다.
실록을 사고에 나누어 보관할 필요가 없었을 것이다.
날씨나 지진 같은 기록은 실록에서 빠졌을 것이다.
challenge.explain: 글은 왕도 기록을 볼 수 없었기 '때문에' 사관이 사실을 있는 그대로 남길 수 있었다고 했다. 이를 뒤집으면, 왕이 기록을 볼 수 있었다면 화낸 일이나 실수까지 그대로 적기는 어려웠을 것이다. 사고에 나누어 보관한 것은 불이나 전쟁으로부터 책을 지키기 위한 일이라, 왕이 기록을 보는 것과는 관계가 없다.

en: In the Joseon Dynasty, an officer called a sagwan stayed near the king. The sagwan wrote down every word and action of the king. He also wrote when the king got angry or made a mistake. Even the king could not read these records freely. So the sagwan could write down the truth.

When a king died, an office called Sillokcheong was set up. Officials gathered the sagwan's records and made a big history book. This book is the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty. It holds politics, weather, earthquakes, and the daily life of people. Almost every day of the Joseon Dynasty is in it.

Joseon kept the finished Annals in storehouses called sago. People made many copies and put them in far places. If one place burned, the books in other places were safe. In a big war, some sago really did burn. But people made new copies from the books that were left.
In 1997, the Annals became a UNESCO Memory of the World. Few countries kept hundreds of years of history so carefully. The world praised Joseon's great culture of writing records.
enseg: and made a big history book.
and put them in far places.
from the books that were left.

questions.q: 이 글의 중심 내용으로 가장 알맞은 것은?

questions.explain: 넷째 문단에서 해례본 덕분에 한글이 어떤 원리로 만들어졌는지 알 수 있다고 하였다.

challenge.q: 이 글의 원리대로 ㅁ에 획을 더해 새 글자를 만들었다면, 그 글자에 대한 설명으로 가장 알맞은 것은?
choices: 하늘과 땅과 사람을 서로 합쳐 만든 글자이다.

challenge.explain: 자음은 기본 글자에 획을 더해 더 센 소리의 글자를 만들었다. ㄱ에 획을 더해 ㅋ을 만든 것처럼, ㅁ에 획을 더한 글자도 ㅁ보다 센 소리를 적는 글자가 된다. '배우기 쉽게'는 세종대왕이 훈민정음 전체를 만든 목적이지 획을 더한 까닭이 아니므로, ㅁ보다 배우기 쉽게 만들었다는 설명은 알맞지 않다.

challenge.q: 백성들이 훈민정음을 쉽게 익힐 수 있었던 까닭으로 가장 알맞은 것은?
choices: 적은 수의 기본 글자와 글자를 만드는 방법만 알면 여러 글자를 알 수 있었기 때문이다.

훈민정음 해례본을 읽으며 글자의 원리를 공부할 수 있었기 때문이다.

en: King Sejong made Hunminjeongeum in 1443. The name means the right sounds to teach the people. Back then, people found Chinese characters very hard to learn. So King Sejong made letters that anyone could learn easily.

The basic consonants copy the shape of our speech parts. The letter ㄱ shows the tongue blocking the throat. The letter ㄴ shows the tongue touching the upper gum. ㅁ copies the mouth, ㅅ the teeth, and ㅇ the throat. Adding a stroke to these five letters makes a stronger sound. For example, ㄱ with one more stroke becomes ㅋ.

The vowels copy the sky, the earth, and people. A round dot means the sky. The flat line ㅡ means the earth. The standing line ㅣ means a person standing up. Joining these three shapes makes many different vowels. So a few basic letters can write many sounds.

A book called Hunminjeongeum Haerye explains how the letters were made. Thanks to this book, we know the rules behind Hangeul. Few writing systems tell us the maker, the year, and the rules. In 1997, the Haerye book became a UNESCO Memory of the World.

en: A webtoon is a comic you read on the internet. It really started in Korea in the early 2000s. At first anyone could read it free, so many people enjoyed it. Unlike a paper comic book, you scroll the screen down. People call this way vertical scroll.

Vertical scroll fits a smartphone very well. You can read it easily with just one finger. The pictures flow from top to bottom, so the story feels smooth. A long empty space can build tension before a surprise. Paper comics did not have this new way.

Webtoons have grown into a big industry. Writers make the stories, and platforms bring them to readers. As readers grew, many new jobs appeared around webtoons. Many popular webtoons become dramas or movies. One story can grow into many different shapes.

Korean webtoons are translated into many languages. Readers in other countries enjoy them on their phones. The vertical scroll way is now used all over the world. A comic style from Korea changed how the world reads comics.

en: Tiny bits of strong energy fly through space. We cannot see them with our eyes. People call them space radiation. On Earth, thick air and a magnetic field block them. But the Moon has almost no air. So space radiation pours right onto the Moon's surface.

You cannot see or feel space radiation. But too much of it can hurt the human body. Someday people may stay on the Moon for a long time. First we must know how strong the radiation there is. Then we can find ways to keep astronauts safe.

Korean scientists are building a machine to measure this radiation. Its name is LVRAD. An American company is making a lander for the Moon. LVRAD will ride on that lander. The plan is to land at the Moon's south pole in 2030. Many countries want to explore the Moon's south pole.

In August 2026, Korea's space agency signed a paper with NASA. The paper promises a seat for LVRAD on the lander. The data from the Moon will help people plan future trips. Korean technology is helping the world explore the Moon.

challenge.q: 사탕 공장은 받은 배출권보다 온실가스를 적게 내보냈고, 장난감 공장은 받은 배출권보다 많이 내보냈습니다. 이 글의 내용에 따르면 어떤 일이 일어날까요?
choices: 장난감 공장은 나라에서 배출권을 공짜로 더 받을 수 있다.
사탕 공장은 남은 배출권을 팔 수 있고, 장난감 공장은 모자란 만큼 사야 한다.
사탕 공장은 온실가스를 적게 내보냈으니 이제 배출권이 필요 없다.
두 공장 모두 온실가스를 내보냈으니 똑같이 배출권을 사야 한다.
challenge.explain: 글에서 온실가스를 적게 내보낸 기업은 남은 배출권을 시장에서 팔고, 많이 내보낸 기업은 모자란 만큼 사야 한다고 했어요. 나라가 배출권을 나누어 주는 것은 처음 정한 양까지이므로, 모자란 공장이 공짜로 더 받는다는 첫 번째 선지는 틀렸어요. 배출권을 사는 것은 모자란 공장뿐이니 두 공장이 똑같이 산다는 것도 맞지 않아요.

challenge.q: 배출권 가격이 아주 싸진다면 어떤 일이 생길지 알맞게 짐작한 것은 무엇인가요?
choices: 배출권이 싸지면 기업들은 온실가스를 지금보다 더 열심히 줄일 것이다.
배출권이 싸지면 나라가 정한 온실가스 전체 양도 저절로 늘어난다.
배출권 가격은 한번 정해지면 변하지 않으므로 이런 일은 일어나지 않는다.
스스로 온실가스를 줄이는 대신 싼 배출권을 사려는 기업이 많아질 수 있다.
challenge.explain: 글에서 가격이 오르면 배출권을 사는 데 돈이 많이 들어 기업이 온실가스를 더 열심히 줄인다고 했으니, 반대로 가격이 싸지면 줄이는 대신 사서 해결하려는 기업이 많아질 수 있어요. 첫 번째 선지는 이와 반대되는 짐작이라 틀렸어요. 온실가스 전체 양은 나라가 정하는 것이므로 가격 때문에 저절로 늘어나지 않아요.

en: Big factories and power plants make things and electricity. While they work, they send out greenhouse gases. These gases wrap the Earth like a blanket and hold heat. So the Earth slowly gets hotter. Many countries are looking for ways to cut these gases.

Korea started a plan called emissions trading in 2015. First, the country sets a total amount of gas. Then it shares that amount among companies. Each company gets the right to send out some gas. People call this right an emission permit.

A company that sends out less gas has permits left over. It can sell them to other companies in the market. A company that sends out more gas must buy permits. So companies cut their gases to save money.

Today about 770 Korean companies join this plan. Permit prices go up and down like stock prices. When the price goes up, buying permits costs a lot. So companies try even harder to cut their gases. In this way, the market helps protect the Earth.

바닷속에서 일어난 일이므로 육지의 날씨와는 아무 관계가 없다.
challenge.explain: ① 바닷물의 온도가 평소보다 훨씬 높은 상태가 5일 이상(일주일째) 이어졌으므로 글의 정의에 따라 해양열파로 볼 수 있고, 양식장의 물고기는 높은 수온을 견디지 못해 죽기도 하므로 미리 대비해야 해요. ② '5일'이라는 본문의 말을 쓴 셋째 선지가 그럴듯하지만, 5일 이상 이어지는 것이야말로 해양열파의 조건이므로 평소의 날씨로 본다는 판단은 거꾸로 된 것이에요.

en: In summer, a heat wave comes to the land. The sea can have a heat wave, too. Sometimes the sea water stays much warmer than usual. When this lasts five days or more, we call it a marine heatwave. Sea water does not cool down easily. So a marine heatwave often lasts a long time.

In August 2026, Korea's weather office shared a new study. It looked at the seas around Korea. In the last ten years, marine heatwaves came about 83 days each year. That is 3.7 times more than before. If the Earth keeps getting warmer, they will come more often. They will also grow stronger.

A hot sea changes many things. Fish that like cold water swim away. They look for a cooler sea. Fish in sea farms can die in warm water. A hot sea also sends heat and water vapor into the air. Water vapor is water that turned into gas. This can make heat waves and heavy rain worse on land.

So scientists watch the sea every day. They use satellites and special tools. When the water may get very hot, they warn people early. This helps people keep their fish and farms safe. Cutting greenhouse gases can also slow the warming. Ocean scientists and climate researchers study these changes. Their work is growing more important.

challenge.explain: 이 검사는 암세포가 혈액에 남긴 DNA 조각의 작은 차이를 인공지능이 찾아내는 방식이에요. 조각이 거의 남지 않으면 단서 자체가 없으니 찾기 어려울 거예요. 두 번째 선지가 헷갈리지만, 인공지능은 혈액 데이터 속 차이를 공부해서 배우는 것이므로 단서가 되는 조각이 없다면 공부할 재료도 없어요. 민감도 90.4%는 대장암 연구에서 나온 결과일 뿐 다른 암에도 그대로 적용된다는 보장은 없어요.

en: Cancer is easier to treat when doctors find it early. To check for colon cancer, doctors use an endoscope. An endoscope is a long tube that goes inside the body. Many people feel afraid of this test. Now there is a new way. One small blood test may show the danger of colon cancer.

Our body is made of tiny cells. When cells get old and die, they break apart. They leave small pieces of DNA in our blood. These pieces are called cell-free DNA. Pieces from cancer cells look a little different. Their length and shape are not the same. AI studies blood data from many people. It learns to find these small differences.

A research team at Seoul Asan Hospital tried this test. It found nine out of ten colon cancer patients. That is a score of 90.4 percent. But the test only shows a chance of cancer. It cannot say for sure. Doctors still need an endoscope test to be certain.

An easy test helps people who put off checkups. They can find cancer early and get help. Many people work together to build this tool. Doctors care for the patients. Life scientists study cells and DNA. Computer developers build the medical AI. Do you like science that saves lives? Then watch this field closely.

en: Changdeokgung in Seoul is an old palace. Kings of the Joseon dynasty lived there. Jongmyo is a shrine near the palace. People held special ceremonies there for old kings and queens. Jongmyo became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1995. Changdeokgung joined the list in 1997. Many stones hold up their floors, stairs, and walls.

A research team from the Korea Heritage Service checked the stones. They studied 4,421 stones, one by one. Most of them are granite, a very hard rock. This granite has a soft pink color. The team also drew maps of the buildings. Colors on the maps show where each stone sits.

Why is the home of a stone important? Wind and rain hurt stones over many years. The stones crack and break apart. Workers must change a broken stone for a new one. A wrong stone looks strange, with a different color. This study found the same granite in Seoul's mountains. Inwangsan and Bugaksan hold this pink rock. So workers can find matching stones for future repairs.

Saving old treasures needs the power of science. We call these workers conservation scientists. They use science to study and protect our heritage. Do you love history and science together? Then this job may be perfect for you.

en: Power plants make the electricity we use. But the plants are not spread out evenly. Factories and offices near Seoul use the most power. Yet most big power plants stand in the south. On August 26, 2026, the government shared a new plan. Korea's energy office and the power company made it. Factories pay for electricity, and the price could change by area. The plan splits the country into eleven areas. Southern areas near power plants would pay up to 10 percent less. This is only a plan for now. People are still sharing their ideas about it.

Why did they make this plan? Different prices can move big electricity users. Factories and data centers may go to cheaper areas. Then the country sends less power over long wires. The south may also gain new jobs. Still, some people are not sure. A small price cut may not move a whole company.

This story is not only for power experts. Engineers plan the roads that electricity travels. Business experts choose the best place for a factory. Policy experts write the rules for prices. They all solve this puzzle together. Can you read the ideas hidden in a price? That skill is the first step to these jobs.

en: In August 2026, the Ministry of Education shared big news. Schools will teach AI as a real school subject. Teachers in the classroom will write the textbooks themselves. There will be six books for elementary school. Middle school gets two, and high school gets eight. That makes sixteen new subjects in all.

Korea has three kinds of textbooks. The country writes the first kind by itself. Companies write the second kind, and the country checks it. For the third kind, the local school office gives approval. The new AI books belong to this third kind.

Why do teachers write the books? Teachers meet students in class every day. So they know what is hard for children. They also know what students really need. AI also changes very fast. New tools appear almost every month. So the main book will hold the big ideas. New facts will go into a small extra book. Teachers can update that book again and again.

Some schools will try the new books in 2027. Real classes will start in March 2028. Today's students will be the first readers. Teachers will guide them through the new books. Edtech developers will build tools that help learning. Content makers will explain hard ideas in simple ways. Do these jobs sound fun? Then keep your eyes on this change.

en: Paintings in a museum change slowly over time. Colors fade. Paper turns yellow. Surfaces crack. Conservation science is the work of stopping this damage. It helps art live longer.

A conservator does not start repairs at once. First she studies the artwork closely. She writes down where it is damaged. Sometimes she checks the materials with science tools. Only then does the treatment begin. Korea's national modern art museum has four teams for this work. They are paper, oil painting, sculpture and craft, and material analysis. Together they care for about 8,000 works.

Protecting art before it breaks matters even more. The museum keeps rooms between 18 and 22 degrees. It also keeps humidity between 50 and 70 percent. Light is set for each material. Oil paintings get 150 lux or less. Ink and watercolor paintings get 100 lux or less. Strong light makes colors fade.

Nam June Paik built a tower of 1,003 old TV sets. New parts were no longer sold anywhere. So the museum spent three years on repairs. Workers fixed 737 screens. They kept the shells of 266 more and changed the inside. Saving art needs an artist's eye and a scientist's hands.

en: Pansori is a Korean art form. One singer tells a long story. A drummer keeps the beat. Only two people stand on the stage. But the story can last for hours.

The singer uses three ways. Singing is called chang. Speaking is called aniri. Moving the body is called ballim. The singer holds only a fan. Open, the fan becomes a door. Closed, it becomes a stick or a brush.

The drummer does more than keep time. He makes the story faster or slower. He shouts short words to cheer the singer. An old saying puts the drummer first and the singer second. The drummer matters that much.
The audience has a special place too. People shout short words and join the show. They do not just sit and watch. They help make the stage. Five pansori stories are still sung today.

en: In 2024 the novelist Han Kang won the Nobel Prize in Literature. She is the first Korean writer to do so. But the judges cannot read Korean. What they read was the book in English and in Swedish. A work needs translation before it can reach the world.

Deborah Smith, a British translator, put Han Kang's novel The Vegetarian into English. She studied English literature at university. In 2010 she began to learn Korean. Three years later she started to translate this novel.

She did more than translate. First she rendered about twenty pages and sent them to a British publisher with an offer. After the book came out, she wrote to critics and readers about it. In 2016 the book won the Booker Prize, and the writer and the translator received it together.

The hardest part of translation is a word with no match. Soju, seonsaengnim, and hyeong change their meaning if you force them into English. Smith kept the Korean sounds instead. Deciding what to change and what to keep is the translator's judgment.

en: Painters in Joseon made landscape pictures for a long time. But the mountains were not Korean mountains. They copied the manner of picture books that came from China. Mountains and rivers the painter had never seen filled the paper. Such work is called idea landscape.

Jeong Seon took another path. He travelled to the mountains of his own country. He climbed Geumgangsan and went up Inwangsan again and again. Then he painted what his own eyes had seen. A landscape drawn from a real place is called jingyeong, a true view.

In 1751, at the age of seventy-six, he painted Inwangsan after the rain stopped. The work is Inwangjesaekdo. He pressed dark ink onto the rocks that the rain had turned black. The painting was held privately for a long time. In 2021 the family of the late chairman Lee Kun-hee gave it to the National Museum of Korea. Now anyone can go and see it.

Yet a true view is not a photograph. His Geumgangjeondo of 1734 shows why. You cannot stand in one spot and see all the peaks of Geumgangsan at once. Jeong Seon walked from place to place and set what he saw into one round picture, as if looking down from above. He did not copy what he saw. He arranged it again.

en: In 1794 King Jeongjo began to build a new fortress at Suwon. This fortress is Hwaseong. The work needed countless heavy stones. Jeong Yak-yong designed a lifting device and a strong cart to raise the stones and carry them. They saved much labour and cost, and the fortress was finished in 1796.

After the work ended, the king had the whole process written into a book. It is called the Hwaseong Seongyeok Uigwe. It holds drawings of the fortress, the kind and number of stones used, the names of the workers and the wages they were paid, and what was done on each day. It was printed in 1801.

Over the years Hwaseong fell badly into ruin. Walls and buildings collapsed through the colonial period and the Korean War. When restoration began in the 1970s, the book was what people opened. The drawings and measurements were still there, so the fortress could be brought back to its original form.

A rebuilt structure usually has trouble becoming a World Heritage site. If there is no way to check the original form, restoration turns into guesswork. Hwaseong needed no guesswork. In 1997 it was placed on the UNESCO World Heritage list. A record written two hundred years earlier built the fortress that stands today.

en: What you learn during the day does not become a lasting memory at once. At first it is left for a short while in a part of the brain called the hippocampus. A memory in this state is still weak, so it fades or disappears easily.
For a memory to last, what sits in the hippocampus must move out to the wide surface of the cerebrum. This moving is called memory consolidation. And it happens mostly while we are asleep.

The brain does not simply rest during sleep. It replays, at high speed, the nerve activity that was switched on while you were learning. Scientists call this reactivation, because the memory comes alive again. This replay appears most strongly in the deepest stage of sleep.

So if you cut your sleep after learning, the moving is not finished properly. That is why staying up all night to memorise does not hold. The national mental health portal advises nine to ten hours of sleep a day for children and teenagers. Even after the book is closed, the studying is not yet over.

en: It is easy to think of a trial as something a judge does alone. In Korea, however, there is a criminal trial in which citizens take part directly. It is called a citizen participation trial, and the people who take part in it are called jurors.

You do not become a juror by applying. The court draws jurors at random from a list prepared in advance. Any citizen over the age of twenty may serve, and no special qualification is needed. People in certain jobs, such as lawyers and police officers, cannot serve. The list itself is redrawn every year, compiled at random from resident registration records.

When the trial ends, the jurors gather on their own. This meeting is called deliberation, and the judge does not enter. If the jurors reach one view, that becomes their conclusion. If they do not, they must hear the judge's opinion and then decide by majority. Even then the judge may not say whether the defendant is guilty or not guilty. The conclusion reached in this way is the verdict.

This verdict, however, does not bind the court. The judge may hand down a judgment different from it. One condition is attached instead. At sentencing the judge must tell the defendant what the jurors decided, and if the judgment differs, must explain why. The rule does not force the judge to follow the verdict, yet it makes the verdict impossible to pass over in silence.

en: When a road is built, a forest is cut in two. The place where animals lived, their habitat, is broken apart. The structure that joins the broken pieces again is called an eco-corridor. Some run under the road as tunnels, and some cross over it as bridges. In Korea the first one was built in 1998 on a road through Jirisan, and today there are eighteen inside the national parks: nine tunnels and nine bridges.

The effect can be seen in numbers. When the Korea National Park Service analysed those eighteen corridors, an average of 522 animals a year passed through during the first three years, and after eight years the figure had risen to 675, an increase of about thirty percent. At the fifteen corridors older than five years, roadkill fell by an average of eighteen percent compared with before they were built. The tunnel built at Odaesan in 2013 showed the largest effect of all, a fall of 87.3 percent.

One thing here deserves attention. The effect did not appear at once. Animals do not use an unfamiliar structure straight away. The rise in numbers and the fall in accidents came only after several years had passed. Had these corridors been graded the moment they were finished, every one of them would have been written down as having no effect.

That does not mean building alone is enough. The Ministry of Environment once surveyed all 564 eco-corridors in the country without exception. It then asked for repairs or improvements at 535 of them. In many, grass and trees inside had not grown properly, or the passage was shared with other uses and could not do its own work. Saying a bridge has been built and saying animals cross it are not the same thing.

en: Even when an old object comes out of the ground, the year it was made is usually unknown. Objects of similar shape are grouped together and only their rough order is guessed at. For this reason archaeology prizes above all an object that pins down a date.

In 1971, while a drainage ditch was being dug in Gongju, a tomb built of bricks came to light by chance. In the passage inside the tomb lay two flat stone tablets side by side. They were stones carved with a record of the tomb's owner, that is, memorial tablets.

The king's tablet said that King Sama of Baekje, Great General Yeongdong, died on the seventh day of the fifth month of 523 at the age of sixty-two, and was laid in the tomb on the twelfth day of the eighth month of 525. The queen's tablet said that she died in the twelfth month of 526 and was laid to rest on the twelfth day of the second month of 529, after the three-year mourning was complete. This King Sama is King Muryeong of Baekje.

A single stone bearing dates became a clock for the whole tomb. The objects found inside now had a fixed time of making, and those objects in turn became a ruler for measuring the age of similar objects from other tombs. The tablets are therefore used as reference material for tracing how the tombs and metal craftwork of Baekje changed over time.

en: A digital record does not blur in the slightest when it is copied. It therefore seems that once saved it will last for ever. The truth is the opposite. Left alone, it disappears faster than paper.

There are two reasons. First, the medium that holds the record ages. A disk too becomes unreadable as time passes. Second, the way of opening a file disappears. A file made with an old program can become impossible to open once that program is gone.

The National Archives of Korea therefore repeats two tasks. One is media conversion, moving records from an ageing medium onto a new one; the other is format conversion, changing a form that will vanish into one that will last. When choosing what to store records on, they weigh lifespan and durability along with capacity and cost.

Nor is the format chosen at random. Several formats were compared against nine criteria, and PDF/A was set as the document preservation format. It was approved as an international standard in 2005 and is an open format that anyone may use without payment. A format that opens only with one company's program traps the record along with it when that company disappears.

en: Falling ill in the Joseon period was quite unlike falling ill today. Physicians were gathered in the cities, and remote villages had no one to prepare medicine. Medical books existed, but all were written in classical Chinese, so few people could read them.

Heo Jun, the royal physician, was ordered by King Seonjo to compile a great medical work, and he completed it in 1610. Its name is Donguibogam and it runs to twenty-five volumes, an encyclopaedic medical book gathering the medical writings of China and Korea into one. In 1613 it was printed with wooden type at the royal clinic.

What sets this book apart is the question of whom it was written for. So that people living where physicians and medicines were hard to come by could treat illness themselves, it collected the remedies in common use. It lists 1,403 medicinal materials in all, and for 637 of them the name is also given in Korean script. Only 102 had to be brought in from China.

The numbers make the intention plain. This was not a book meant for scholars alone. The names were made findable by people who could not read Chinese characters, and the ingredients were ones nobody had to import. Because the idea that the state should provide medical care for ordinary people is embodied here earlier than anywhere else, Donguibogam was inscribed as a UNESCO Memory of the World document in 2009.

en: The old way of printing a book was the woodblock. A page's worth of characters was carved whole into a board, ink was applied and paper pressed onto it. Carving took great labour, but it was good for printing the same book again and again. To print a different book, however, the board had to be carved from the beginning.

Metal type turned the idea around. Each character is cast separately in metal; the needed characters are picked out, set into a frame, printed, then broken up and used again. With type made once, many different books can be printed.

The oldest surviving book printed this way is the Jikji. Its full name is Baegun hwasang chorok buljo jikji simche yojeol, and it was printed in 1377 at Heungdeoksa temple in Cheongju. That is seventy-eight years before Gutenberg printed his Bible. In 2001 it was inscribed as a UNESCO Memory of the World document.

One further thing must be seen alongside this: being first is not the same as spreading widely. The Jikji was printed in two volumes, but only the lower one survives, and even that is in the National Library of France. That a technology came earlier, and that the technology changed a society, are two separate stories that have to be checked separately.

en: Houses in cold places and houses in hot places have different problems to solve. A cold place must hold heat in; a hot place must let heat and damp out. For that reason houses in the two are usually built in opposite ways.

The ondol is the device that solves the first problem. When a fire is lit in the kitchen furnace, the heat runs along flues cut beneath the floor and warms the flat stones above them. Once heated, those stones go on giving off warmth long after the fire has died. It is a method that came out of the cold of the north.

The maru solves the second problem. Wooden boards are laid on a floor raised above the ground, so that air passes underneath and damp does not gather. It is a method that came out of the hot, humid south — the exact opposite direction from the ondol.

What marks the hanok is that these two were set side by side in a single building. In winter people lived in the ondol room, in summer on the wide wooden floor of the daecheong. In our climate, where both summer and winter are sharp, the house holds both answers at once. A form in which ondol and maru share one building is rare in the world.

en: In 1559 a young scholar named Gi Daeseung sent a letter to Yi Hwang, then regarded as the finest scholar of the age. He wrote that one line in a diagram Yi Hwang had made did not seem right. Yi Hwang was born in 1501 and Gi Daeseung in 1527, so the objection came first from a man twenty-six years his junior.

The subject of the dispute was the human mind. The four beginnings are four good impulses, such as pitying others and knowing shame; the seven feelings are seven emotions such as joy and anger. Yi Hwang held that the two arise from different sources, while Gi Daeseung held that the four beginnings are contained within the seven feelings.

The two did not meet and settle it face to face. They exchanged letters and carried the debate on until 1566. When one wrote an objection, the other answered with reasons. In the course of it Yi Hwang even revised his own wording.

The end was not victory or defeat. Gi Daeseung composed two pieces setting out his view and sent them, and Yi Hwang judged their content excellent. With that the debate closed. Seong Hon and Yi I later took up the same question, and Korean scholarship deepened by digging into it.

en: A city is hotter than the land around it. Asphalt and concrete soak up heat through the day and give it back until late at night. This is called the heat island effect. Yet even inside one city the temperature differs from district to district.

The National Institute of Forest Science surveyed the twenty-five districts of Seoul. It laid the Korea Forest Service's spatial data on urban forests over satellite images and compared them with summer land surface temperatures. The result was clear: the higher the share of ground covered by trees in a district, the lower its summer surface temperature.
There are two reasons. The shade of a tree blocks strong sunlight, and water leaving the leaves as vapour carries surrounding heat away with it. The two together lower the temperature.

The effect shows even in small trees. Measured with a thermal camera, the shade of street trees was on average two to three degrees cooler than its surroundings, and the shade of trees on traffic islands more than four degrees cooler. It is not a matter of having to build a great forest; a single tree, or a small grove, does its share.

en: Fine dust is divided by size. Particles smaller than ten micrometres across are called fine dust, and those smaller than 2.5 micrometres ultrafine dust. Ultrafine particles are about one twentieth to one thirtieth the width of a human hair. Being so small, they are not filtered out in the airway and travel deep into the lungs.

Concentrations are therefore forecast every day. For ultrafine dust the amount contained in a cubic metre of air is measured and reported in four grades: good, moderate, bad and very bad. Zero to fifteen is good, sixteen to thirty-five moderate, thirty-six to seventy-five bad, and seventy-six or above very bad.

One thing here deserves notice: each grade covers a wide span. Thirty-six is bad and seventy-five is also bad, yet in numbers they differ by more than double. Very bad has no upper limit at all. Under the same name, the amount reaching the body can be very different.

Grades are useful for telling us quickly what to be careful about that day. Look only at the grade, however, and the differences inside it stay invisible. That is why it is worth reading the number as well. Children, older people, pregnant women and anyone with a weak respiratory system or heart need to take care earlier than others.

en: An antibiotic is a medicine that kills bacteria. Thanks to it, illnesses that once took lives are now cured in a few days. Yet this medicine has a property no other drug shares: the more it is used, the less it works.

The reason lies on the bacterial side. When an antibiotic is used, most bacteria die, but those on which the drug works poorly survive. With their competitors gone, they multiply, and the drug steadily loses its force. Bacteria that a drug no longer affects are called resistant bacteria.

Here a mismatch appears. For a single patient, getting well quickly now is best. For society as a whole, keeping the drug effective for a long time is best. The two bests do not always point the same way.

The government therefore handles this problem across several ministries. Seven of them took part in the plan drawn up in 2026, because it is not only people that must be managed but animals, food and the environment as well. Hospitals check that antibiotics are used only as far as necessary, and vaccination is being expanded to reduce how often people fall ill in the first place.

en: Public bodies produce a great deal of data as they work: the live position of buses, the location of hospitals and pharmacies, weather and prices. Collecting it costs tax money.

There was always a way to see such data. You could file a request for disclosure. That route, however, moves only when somebody asks. You have to know what exists before you can ask for it, and what comes back is usually in a form meant for human eyes.

Open public data runs the other way. Rather than waiting to be asked, the data is posted in one place in advance. More than that, it is released not only for people to read but in a form a program can take and use directly. This difference is decisive.

Because of it, things the government never built came into being — apps that tell you when a bus will arrive, services that find a pharmacy that is open. After the law was made in 2013, the amount of data posted on the public data portal grew greatly, and the number of times it was taken and used grew far more.
